name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,880

clue.text: Pharma giant getting into development of magical pesticide, perhaps

indicators.note: Developing a site means pulling it about and putting it back another way, which is what the letters do here.
A company that gets into something has moved inside it, so these five letters land in the middle of the rest.

blocks.note: seven letters reordered, then split open to take a passenger
Roche of Basel is one of the world's largest drug companies

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells a magic potion and the answer is the industrial reality. When a clue says 'pharma giant' it usually wants a real company's name, and that is a habit worth acquiring.
explanation.definitionFit: A pesticide is one kind of agrochemical, the umbrella word for the chemicals farming uses, so 'perhaps' flags a definition by example.

clue.text: Bellyache from drinking rum punch

indicators.note: Here the word points at a source you draw something out of, so the answer is already sitting in the words that follow.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters spanning the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.walkthrough: A rum punch is a real drink, which is exactly what stops you counting letters. Hidden answers hide best inside phrases that read as ordinary English, and this one reads as a complaint about a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are nouns for a moan: a bellyache is a whinge, and the answer is the sulky grumble a bad-tempered person indulges in.

clue.text: Exclude East German breed taking lead in Crufts?

indicators.note: One piece takes another in the sense of swallowing it, so the new letter goes inside rather than alongside.
The lead of a word is the letter standing at its front, and dogs are led as well, which is what keeps the surface honest.

blocks.note: 'Ost' is simply German for east
a farmer who breeds animals raises them
the leading letter of the dog show's name

explanation.walkthrough: 'East German breed' is trying hard to look like a dog — an Alsatian, say — and Crufts, Britain's national dog show, keeps the picture going. Neither phrase is naming a breed at all.
explanation.definitionFit: To ostracise someone is to shut them out of a group by common consent, which is precisely what excluding them means.

clue.text: Someone who has quit company misusing HR time

indicators.note: To misuse a thing is to put it to the wrong job, and letters put to the wrong job come back in the wrong order.

blocks.note: six letters — the personnel department plus a word for a spell

explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' is the pivot. On the surface it is the firm whose HR department is meant; in the definition it means other people's society. Note that the fodder is handed over as an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit is a recluse who has withdrawn from society altogether, so the definition names the person by what they walked away from.

clue.text: Gunman maybe spinning barrel before start of roulette

indicators.note: A cylinder that spins comes round to face the other way, so those letters are read in the opposite direction.
It asks only for the letter a word begins with, never for the word itself.

blocks.note: a barrel is a drum, and the spin turns those four letters round
'ere' is the old poetic word for before
the leading letter of roulette

explanation.walkthrough: Everything on the surface belongs to a revolver and a casino, but the barrel wanted is the wooden kind. 'Gunman maybe' is definition by example — one sort of the answer, not the only one.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunman who kills is one instance of the wider word, which is what 'maybe' signals: the answer covers every method, not only shooting.

clue.text: Intriguing group from California set up research establishment

indicators.note: In a down entry, setting something up stands it on end, so those letters climb back the way they came.

blocks.note: CA is the postal abbreviation for California
a research establishment is a lab, stood on its head here

explanation.walkthrough: 'Intriguing' is not the adjective it looks like. It means engaged in intrigue — plotting — rather than fascinating, and that shift is the whole of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabal is a small group that meets in secret to scheme, so 'intriguing' carries its literal sense of plotting rather than fascinating.

clue.text: Girl hosts banal ceremony before popping off

indicators.note: A host keeps guests inside the house, so one word here takes another in and closes around it.

blocks.note: a lass is a girl, chiefly in northern British use
something banal is trite — worn out by repetition

explanation.walkthrough: 'Popping off' is British slang for dying, so the definition reads on the surface like a send-off before somebody nips out for a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: The last rites are the prayers a priest gives someone who is dying, so the ceremony really does come immediately before death.

clue.text: To run successful budget, introduce limits?

blocks.note: to introduce two people is to make them meet, which supplies both outer words at once
the limits of anything are its ends

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: 'introduce limits' sounds like a Treasury announcement, and the definition sounds like more of the same. Both halves talk about money, which is why the seam is so hard to find.
explanation.definitionFit: Making ends meet is the idiom for spending no more than you earn, which is exactly what running a household budget successfully amounts to.

clue.text: Screen that opens in silence, say

blocks.note: 'sh' is the sound you make to hush somebody
to say something is to utter it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Silence, say' looks like one phrase asking for an example of quiet, and it is really two separate instructions standing side by side. The comma is the setter's only warning.
explanation.definitionFit: A shutter is the hinged panel fitted across a window, and its whole purpose is to swing open and shut — a screen that does exactly that.

clue.text: Taps in expensive rental run with water periodically

indicators.note: Here the little word is an instruction rather than joinery: what comes before it is placed inside what comes after.

blocks.note: a steep price is an expensive one
a lease is the rental agreement on a property
a sink has two taps, cold and hot, and those are their letters

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole of the tail, not just 'run': the water is the jump the athletes clear once every lap. Plumbing runs right through the surface, which is what hides the pair of taps.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeplechase is a distance race whose every lap includes a water jump, so it really is a run that meets water at regular intervals.

clue.text: Coach breaks work schedule for coffee

indicators.note: Something that breaks into a thing forces its way inside and splits it, which is where the shorter piece ends up.

blocks.note: a rota is the British word for the list saying who works when
a coach is a long-distance bus

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a driver's tea break and the definition is a single word at the far end. 'Coach' is capitalised only because it opens the clue, not because it is anybody's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Robusta is one of the two species of bean the world drinks, alongside arabica, so the plain word 'coffee' names it by its kind.

clue.text: Underline M representing magnitude in report

indicators.note: Something given in report is being repeated as spoken, so what you are handed is a sound to write down some other way.

blocks.note: one thing representing another stands for it
magnitude is size — how big a thing is
the letter is said 'em', and the three spoken words run together into one

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is anagrammed or hidden here. The clue asks you to read three words aloud and hear a fourth, and 'M for size' said at speed is the whole mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: Underlining a word on the page is how writing gives it extra weight, and that is precisely the job this verb names.

clue.text: What leads Veronica into temptation? Affection, ironically

indicators.note: What leads a word is the letter standing at its head, the one that goes in front of all the others.
It marks a placement rather than a journey: the single letter is dropped inside the longer word.

blocks.note: a lure is the bait that tempts, so the noun and it come to the same thing
the leading letter of the name

explanation.walkthrough: The clue borrows the Lord's Prayer for its surface — lead us not into temptation — and the question mark owns up to the borrowing. 'Ironically' is the setter admitting the spelling is a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the deliberately gushy, over-sung spelling of love, so it means affection while the misspelling supplies the irony the clue admits to.

clue.text: Doctor sips at aperitif

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it, and letters tampered with come back rearranged.

blocks.note: six letters, taken from the two words and reordered

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor sips' reads as a sentence about a medic having a drink, which is the neatest kind of anagram surface: indicator and fodder disguised as subject and verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastis is the aniseed spirit drunk before dinner in the south of France, which is exactly the job an aperitif does.

clue.text: Wicket-keepers perhaps, who can be difficult to get out?

definitions.text: Wicket-keepers perhaps, who can be difficult to get out?

blocks.note: the surface is cricket, where the keeper crouches behind the stumps all day; but a wicket is also a small gate, and the people who keep one are not fielders

blocks.clueFragment: who can be difficult to get out?
blocks.note: in cricket getting someone out means dismissing the batter; in a building it means eviction, and the law makes that slow

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to unpick here, only two readings of one sentence. Move it off the cricket field and into an empty house and every word in it changes job.
explanation.definitionFit: People who move into an empty property without permission crouch on ground that is not theirs and are notoriously slow to evict — both readings at once.

clue.text: Intensify stock cube using chicken

indicators.note: A word that uses another has it in hand, so the shorter piece is held inside the longer one.

blocks.note: a hen is the chicken of the henhouse, the female bird
two cubed — a cube here is arithmetic, not a shape
surface only: it welds the cube and the chicken into a kitchen ingredient, and contributes no letters

explanation.walkthrough: A chicken stock cube is exactly the picture the setter wants in your head, and 'stock' is the one word in the clue with no job to do beyond painting it.
explanation.definitionFit: To heighten a feeling is to raise its pitch, which is what intensifying does — the word survives mostly in this figurative sense rather than about physical height.

clue.text: These perhaps disturbed eelgrass catching prey finally

definitions.text: These perhaps disturbed eelgrass catching prey finally

indicators.note: Seagrass that has been disturbed is churned up and no longer lying as it was, which is what happens to these letters.
A thing catching something has taken it in, so an extra letter joins the pile being churned about.
It asks for the last letter of the word in front of it, the one that comes at the finish.

blocks.note: eight letters of seagrass, waiting to be reordered
the last letter of the word, added to the shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, the sentence describes real animals foraging in a seagrass bed; read as instructions, the same words build the answer. Doing both at once is what makes a clue an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole sentence reads straight as a description of the animals: they really do churn up seagrass beds while hunting fish, and 'these perhaps' points at them.

clue.text: Tailors around close to Royal Academy's area

indicators.note: One word goes round the other like a coat, so the shorter piece ends up in the middle of the longer.

blocks.note: a garment that has been tailored fits, and the verb works the same way
close to something is near it

explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Academy of Arts is the London institution whose summer exhibition fills its walls with painting and sculpture, so the definition is pointing at a discipline rather than a place.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine arts are painting, sculpture and their relatives — the disciplines a Royal Academy exists to exhibit and teach, so this really is its field.

clue.text: Pale green used by teenage Auden illegibly

indicators.note: A colour used by something is being carried around inside it, so the letters are already sitting in the words that follow.

blocks.note: eight unbroken letters, running from the end of the first word straight through the second and into the third

explanation.walkthrough: 'Illegibly' is planted to look like an anagram instruction, and it cannot be one — its own letters are part of what is being concealed. The poet's name sits in the middle untouched.
explanation.definitionFit: Eau de nil is French for 'water of the Nile', the soft grey-green shade decorators and dressmakers have been using for a century.

clue.text: On the radio, maybe hear America's checking who's in the country

indicators.note: What comes over the air is heard and never seen, so the clue is describing a sound and leaving you to spell it.

blocks.note: hearing is one of the five senses, which is what 'maybe' flags
US is the everyday abbreviation for America
the two words said one after the other make a single spoken word

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s does two jobs at once: it makes 'America's' possessive on the surface, and it carries the verb 'is' in the reading that matters. Everything after it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A census is the official head-count of everyone resident, so it is precisely the exercise of checking who is in a country at a given moment.

clue.text: Car repairs botched with loss of power

indicators.note: A botched job has come out wrong and misshapen, which is what happens to letters put back in the wrong order.
It marks a letter that leaves before the shuffling starts, rather than one joining in.

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for power, and it is dropped before anything else happens
the seven letters minus that one, rearranged into six

explanation.walkthrough: The Ford Sierra was the family car on every British driveway in the 1980s, so 'Car' defines it by example. The surface reads as a botched repair that cost the engine its power.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sierra was a Ford model sold in Britain for a decade, so the general word 'Car' points at it as one instance.

clue.text: Leave egg where food is served

blocks.note: what a chick does when it breaks out of the shell
the opening in a wall between kitchen and dining room, with a shelf for the plates

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses that share nothing but a spelling, in a clue five words long with no joinery at all, so the only question worth asking is where the seam falls.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the chick breaking out of its shell; the other is the serving hatch, that opening between a kitchen and the room next door.

clue.text: Permit I see to put up tiny building on Park Lane?

indicators.note: In a down entry, putting something up sends it back the way it came, so the assembled letters are read from the bottom.

blocks.note: to let a flat is to permit its use for rent
'oh' is the noise of understanding, the spoken form of 'I see'

explanation.walkthrough: Park Lane is the dark-blue square at the expensive end of the British Monopoly board, and what you put on it is a small plastic block — which is what makes 'tiny building' fair.
explanation.definitionFit: In Monopoly you buy houses and then a hotel for a square like Park Lane, so the answer really is a tiny building placed there.

clue.text: French composer recalled job on island in Ireland

indicators.note: To recall a thing is to call it back, and letters called back are read the other way round.
It puts what comes before it inside what comes after, rather than merely joining the two together.

blocks.note: Eire is the Irish name for the Republic, and it opens up to take the rest
I is the map abbreviation for island
a job you are given to do is a task

explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are assembled the right way round and only then turned over, which is why no part of the answer looks like any of them. Satie is the composer of the Gymnopedies.
explanation.definitionFit: Erik Satie wrote the Gymnopedies, so the definition names only a nationality and a trade and leaves you to supply the man.

clue.text: Police force raised detective's rates

indicators.note: A down entry that is raised reads from the bottom upwards, so those letters arrive in the opposite order.

blocks.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police, stood on its head here
a PI is a private investigator, the detective for hire

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rates' means speeds here rather than charges, and the surface is pretending to be about pay. The answer is the Italian plural of tempo, which is why it ends the way it does.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempi are the speeds at which pieces of music are played, and a speed is a rate — the Italian plural of tempo, kept whole in English.

clue.text: Husband and wife changing in tent, perhaps are too hot

indicators.note: Changing one thing for another is a swap, so a letter here is not removed but replaced by a different one.

blocks.note: a tent is one kind of shelter, which is what 'perhaps' is flagging
H is the standard abbreviation for husband, and it is the letter that goes
W is the standard abbreviation for wife, and it takes the vacated place

explanation.walkthrough: Getting changed in a tent is a whole camping holiday in four words, and it conceals an instruction to swap one letter for another. Both letters are the crossword's usual shorthand for the two people.
explanation.definitionFit: To swelter is to suffer oppressive heat, so the phrase describes people in exactly the state this verb names.

clue.text: Let back in to lecture at American uni

blocks.note: to read a paper to an audience is to deliver it, the old sense of lecturing
the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, known everywhere by its initials

explanation.walkthrough: 'Let back in' opens the clue, which is the awkward place for a definition and the reason it reads as part of the story. Nothing is reversed here despite the word 'back'.
explanation.definitionFit: To readmit somebody is to let them in again after they have been turned out, the RE- prefix carrying the sense of going back.

clue.text: Mincing Spanish males marketing art

indicators.note: Mincing chops a thing into small pieces which are then pressed back together in a new shape.

blocks.note: twelve letters, taken from the two words and reordered

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mincing' is placed to describe how the Spanish males walk rather than what becomes of their letters, which is the oldest trick in the anagram book and still a good one.
explanation.definitionFit: Salesmanship is the skill of persuading people to buy, which is what marketing is an art of — the noun names the craft, not the trade.
